question: The Work Explorer and the CLI checklist cannot say which step a session is currently on, because no writer ever produces an in-progress step status. Should the missing state be WRITTEN by a new or extended writer, or DERIVED at read time from rows both surfaces already read?
decision: Derive, never write. The active step is computed in the one Python row derivation (build_rows) and its TypeScript mirror as the lowest-numbered seeded plan-step row with nothing logged against it, in a session session-state.json reports as in flight. No writer changes, and nothing is stored on disk to make it true.

options.option: Derive it at read time from the seeded plan rows plus session-state.json (Option 2 in the source-of-record note).
options.consequence: No writer change and no orchestrator convention to remember; it cannot drift out of sync because it is computed from the same rows the tree already reads; and it fixes every historical set retroactively. Costs a second implementation of the predicate (Python and TypeScript), which is why a cross-language parity falsifier is scheduled in Session 2.

options.option: Option 1 from the note: log an in_progress entry on ENTERING each step.
options.consequence: Doubles every log_step call and depends on an orchestrator convention this repo keeps having to replace with a gate; the on-disk evidence (in-progress is ~1.4% of every step status ever written, and appears in no current set) is what that convention already decayed to. Fixes nothing historical, and adds a writer that can drift from reality whenever a session dies mid-step.

options.option: Option 3 from the note: start_session stamps step 1 as in-progress.
options.consequence: Option 1 with extra steps, and wrong from step 2 onward -- it would assert the session is on step 1 for the entire session. Fixes nothing historical and adds a state-file-adjacent writer for a display concern.

rationale: Taken at spec authoring (docs/session-sets/127-the-active-step-shows-in-progress/spec.md, Scope: 'Option 2 from the note -- derive it'), journalled at Session 1 registration with the spec cited as origin. prefer-reversible decides it: a pure read-time derivation can be deleted in one commit and leaves no residue on disk, while a new writer's output becomes historical record the moment it runs and cannot be un-written from sets that already closed. goal-over-letter points the same way -- the goal is that the operator can see where a session is, including in sets that closed months ago, and only the derivation reaches those. The rejected options are recorded here so they are not re-opened mid-set.

question: The derived in-flight step state is a new signal in a workflow full of machine-enforced gates. Should it be allowed to affect anything other than what is shown to the operator -- an exit code, the log_step vocabulary, or a close gate?
decision: Display-only. The derived state changes no exit code, adds nothing to the log_step status vocabulary, and nothing is stored on disk. It is read by the checklist renderer, the projection, and the tree, and by nothing that decides whether a session may close.

options.option: Display-only: the derivation reaches renderers and the projection, and no gate, exit code, or writer.
options.consequence: The blast radius is what an operator sees. A wrong derivation shows a wrong glyph, which is bad but visible and instantly fixable; it cannot refuse a close or corrupt a record. Keeps the change deletable in one commit.

options.option: Let the derived state feed a gate (e.g. refuse to close while a step is derived in flight, or warn on an exit code).
options.consequence: Would make a derived, heuristic signal load-bearing for close-out. A derivation that is wrong on an edge case would then block real work, and callers and CI would adapt to the new exit code, making it expensive to walk back.

options.option: Add in-progress to the log_step status vocabulary so the derivation and the writer share one token.
options.consequence: Re-opens the rejected write-it option through the side door, and re-introduces the convention the derivation exists to remove.

rationale: Taken at spec authoring (docs/session-sets/127-the-active-step-shows-in-progress/spec.md, Session 1 Step 1 and the 'No new writer' non-goal), journalled at Session 1 registration with the spec cited as origin. prefer-reversible decides it: keeping a new signal out of every gate and exit code is what makes the whole set removable, and it bounds the worst case of a mis-derivation to a wrong glyph rather than a refused close. This decision REDUCES nothing about verification -- it withholds a new signal from the gates rather than weakening an existing check -- so it is not a verification-reduction call and remains AI-authored.

question: How should the derived step start time be scoped -- does each row also carry an end time, does the display handle sessions that cross midnight, and does a row that has not started show its seeded registration timestamp?
decision: Start time only, no date handling, and no time at all on a row that has not started. A finished step's end is the next row's start one line below it; a session crossing midnight is left to the reader (the next row's hour being smaller says the day rolled over); a seeded plan row's dateTime is registration time and must never render as a start.

options.option: Start only, no date, nothing on an unstarted row (the operator's ruling).
options.consequence: One narrow grey field per started row. No duplicate data, no width spent on a case most sets never hit, and no risk of presenting a registration timestamp as a start -- which would be a fresh wrong signal of exactly the kind this set exists to remove.

options.option: Render start and end on every row.
options.consequence: Duplicate data on every row for no added information, since a finished step's end is already the next row's start.

options.option: Add date handling for sessions that cross midnight.
options.consequence: Costs width on every row to disambiguate a rare case, and the giveaway (a smaller hour on the next row) is already free.

options.option: Show the seeded row's own dateTime on an unstarted row.
options.consequence: Renders registration time as if it were a start -- a new wrong signal, worse than the silence this set is fixing.

operator_attestation: Operator rulings taken 2026-08-12 at spec authoring and recorded in docs/session-sets/127-the-active-step-shows-in-progress/spec.md under 'Operator rulings on the timestamp -- settled, do not reopen'; journalled verbatim at Session 1 registration.
rationale: These are display value trade-offs (information density versus row width versus the risk of a misleading signal) with no derivable right answer, so they are the operator's to make, and they were made at authoring. Journalled here as required by Session 1 Step 1 so the settled answers travel with the set and are not re-opened by a later session or a verifier. Session 2 renders these rulings; the UAT walk is where the operator sees the result of them, which is why this entry is tagged for the Decide section.

question: This session's Creates line names a `<slug>-uat-checklist.json`, but the repo's canonical UAT artifact since Set 110 is the guided-look walk doc (`sN-uat-walk.md`, as shipped by Sets 111, 112 and 115) and it is the only artifact `check_uat_walk_recorded` reads. Which does this set produce?
decision: The walk doc, `s2-uat-walk.md`, and not a checklist JSON. It is authored in this session because this is the session that changed the surface, and it is offered to the operator now; the `uatScope: per-set` gate places the recorded obligation on session 3, which references this file from `disposition.uat.walkArtifact`.

options.option: Author `s2-uat-walk.md` in the current guided-look format and let session 3 record it.
options.consequence: One artifact, one sign-off, in the format the close gate actually reads and the format the operator has walked three times. The spec's own rationale asks for exactly this shape -- 'a single guided look, not a tour' -- so the letter of the Creates line is the only thing that differs.

options.option: Produce the `<slug>-uat-checklist.json` the Creates line names, instead of a walk.
options.consequence: Follows the spec's letter and produces an artifact no close gate reads. The extension's uatBadge would render a count, but the operator's sign-off would live in a file the workflow no longer walks, which is how a UAT evaporates while looking complete.

Two artifacts for one sign-off. The authoring guide names conflated sign-off as an anti-pattern in the neighbouring direction (re-using a prior set's checklist), and the same objection applies: a reviewer cannot tell which one the operator actually answered.

rationale: goal-over-letter decides it. The goal named in the spec's own rationale is that the operator who reported the defect looks at the real thing and says whether the icon now answers their question; the guided-look walk is the format that does that, is what `check_uat_walk_recorded` reads, and is what Sets 111/112/115 shipped. The Creates line names an older artifact shape, which is a spec-vs-reality conflict rather than a scope change -- nothing is added or cut, only the file that carries the same sign-off. Surfaced at Step 9 rather than fixed silently, and journalled here so a verifier reading the spec's Creates line sees why the file it names is absent. This decision does NOT reduce verification: the automated half (Layer 3 rendering assertions) is unchanged and ran first, per project-guidance's rule that everything automation can check is checked before the human is asked.

question: Session 1's verification left one adjudicated-minor residual for this session to own: the start-time chain reads a logged entry's `dateTime` as its step's completion even when that entry's status is not a recognised terminal token. Should the chain require a terminal status before advancing?
decision: No. The chain advances on the ENTRY EXISTING, not on what its status says, in both languages. `log_step` writes when the orchestrator records the step, so its stamp is the last known moment of that step's activity and the best available lower bound for the row below it. Pinned by the corpus case `the-start-time-chain-does-not-read-the-status-vocabulary` and documented in both `_completion_of` docstrings.

options.option: Keep the current rule: any logged entry's dateTime advances the chain.
options.consequence: The start times stay independent of the status vocabulary, which this module already refuses to trust in the other direction. Legacy sets spelling completion `completed` (one of the 15 non-canonical tokens Set 120 S2 deliberately preserved, which the renderer boxes `[?]`) keep their start times. One rule, one predicate, no second table of tokens.

options.option: Advance the chain only on a status the box table recognises as terminal.
options.consequence: Reads stricter and is strictly worse in practice: every legacy set whose steps say `completed`, `done`-by-prose, or one of the other preserved tokens silently loses every start time, and the derivation would then be trusting a status field it explicitly does not trust when deciding the active step. It also adds a second token table beside the one that already exists (L-069-1).

options.option: Break the chain on a non-terminal status the same way an unclaimed planned row breaks it.
options.consequence: Symmetrical on paper, but the shape it targets cannot mislead: a row that says `in-progress` makes the record the answer, so no planned row below it is ever derived active, and a planned row that is not active carries no time at all. The only ledger where it would change anything is a self-contradictory one (a step logged in-progress followed by a step logged complete), and answering `unknown` there is not better than answering the last recorded moment.

rationale: simpler-code decides it, and goal-over-letter agrees. The stricter rule adds a second vocabulary table for no reachable gain and takes a real, measurable loss on legacy sets. It is recorded here rather than left implicit because Session 1's disposition named this session as the residual's owner, and settling it in both languages at once is exactly why it was deferred here rather than split across two verification rounds. verification_effect is `strengthens`: the settlement ships with a cross-language corpus case that fires on the disputed shape, where before the behaviour was untested in either language.

question: The checklist gate requires a post inside each verification-round transition's own positional window, but a blocking discovery round drives `discovery -> supplementary -> remediate -> remediation-review` minutes apart, machine-driven, with no human at the terminal -- so those posts are missed repeatedly (Set 126 S2 missed rounds 2 and 3), a miss cannot be repaired, and the only exit is an operator waiver. Should the round-boundary post be automated inside `verify_session`, left to orchestrator discipline, or should the gate be re-armed as blocking?
decision: Option 1 -- auto-render. `verify_session` renders the checklist itself at the end of every round that actually completed, in every phase, through the existing `record_post` path, so the record still means a render happened. A refused round (past the bound), a routed-call failure, and `--dry-run` record nothing. The gate's positional-window rule is unchanged and every other transition type (test-run recorded, operator stop, last logged step) keeps binding exactly as it does today.

options.consequence: Eliminates the failure mode rather than adding discipline to it (project-guidance: prefer removal over addition), and the round output becomes more informative because the operator sees where the session is at each boundary. The cost is that the verification-round transition loses its diagnostic value: it can no longer be missed, so it can no longer report a missing post. That is a reduction in what a close-time gate can catch, which is why this is the operator's call and not the orchestrator's.

options.option: Orchestrator discipline only -- change nothing, keep asking the orchestrator to remember.
options.consequence: Keeps every transition type diagnostic, and keeps failing on the exact sequence where no human is watching. The prose version of this obligation already decayed once in Set 111 S4, which is why the gate exists at all; Set 126 S2 shows the same decay under the gate. A recurring, structurally predictable omission keeps landing on the operator's desk as paperwork.

options.option: Re-arm the gate as blocking (it is advisory by the Set 116 S3 operator ruling).
options.consequence: Strongest signal of the three, and the only one that would force the miss to be dealt with rather than noted. It would also have refused Set 126 S2's close outright and forced a waiver for a paperwork miss the orchestrator could not have filed mid-remediation -- turning a reporting gap into a close-time blocker on the least-attended part of the loop.

operator_attestation: Operator ratified Option 1 on 2026-08-12 at Session 3 registration, in the education-mode brief required by the spec's 'The one decision Session 3 must have ratified before it starts'. The two rejected options and their consequences are recorded above as the spec requires.
rationale: This decision reduces what a close-time gate can catch, which is the hard carve-out the decision-rights rubric reserves to the operator and `decision_journal` refuses to let the orchestrator self-authorize. It is journalled before any Session 3 implementation because a session that starts before the answer exists is implementing an unratified change to a gate. The reduction is deliberately narrow: one transition type inside one gate, with the window rule, the waiver path, and every other transition type untouched -- Session 3's falsifiers assert that narrowness in both directions.
